edge_cases.label: Good: Measurement plan written before launch, whole chain with stated gaps
edge_cases.description: A pre-launch measurement plan for a new-manager programme with an objective-to-evidence table, baseline and delayed measures, a staggered comparison, measured workplace conditions, and decision thresholds set in advance.
edge_cases.input: Measurement plan for a new-manager programme. Two cohorts of 12. Written before launch and agreed with the sponsor. Stage: pre_launch.
edge_cases.artifact:
MEASUREMENT PLAN - New Manager Programme (agreed with the sponsor before launch)

DECISION THIS INFORMS: whether to run the programme for the next two intakes as is, revise it, or retire it. Decision owner: Head of People Development. Decision date: 14 weeks after cohort 2 ends.

OBJECTIVE-TO-EVIDENCE TABLE
O1 Hold a feedback conversation using the SBI structure.
  Learning: role-play checklist score (two trained raters, agreement checked in the pilot at 0.82).
  Behavior: senior-manager observation checklist at 30 and 90 days; sample of 1:1 notes, with consent.
  Results: engagement survey item 7 ('I get useful feedback from my manager'), next two cycles.
  Source and owner: learning record store - L&D; engagement survey - HR analytics (access confirmed).
O2 Delegate a task with a stated outcome, deadline, and check-in point.
  Learning: scenario 4 decisions. Behavior: delegation log sampled at 30 and 90 days. Results: none planned; no team-level measure isolates delegation, and we say so.
O3 Run a weekly 1:1 with every direct report.
  Learning: not measured (a scheduling habit, not a skill). Behavior: calendar system counts at baseline, 30, and 90 days. Results: same engagement item as O1.

CHAIN: participation and reaction are recorded but kept to one page; reaction is not used as evidence of learning. Results for O2 are deliberately not measured (reason above).

TIMING: baseline four weeks before the programme; end of programme; 30 days; 90 days.
SAMPLE: 2 cohorts, 24 managers. Because the group is small we report counts and cases, not percentages. Expected observation coverage: at least 20 of 24; managers not observed are listed with the reason.

COMPARISON: cohort 2 starts ten weeks after cohort 1 and serves as its comparison at the 30-day point. Engagement item 7 is tracked for the four prior cycles so an existing trend is not read as an effect. Success Case Method interviews with the three strongest and three weakest transfer cases after day 90. Other explanations we will check: the pay review in month 3, the new HR system, and manager turnover.

WORKPLACE CONDITIONS: each participant's senior manager attends a 45-minute briefing, gets a one-page observation guide, and reports at 30 and 90 days. Weekly 1:1s are put in calendars before the programme ends. Follow-up prompts at weeks 2, 5, and 9, each revisiting the commitment the manager wrote down. The two barriers named in the needs analysis (no protected time; span of control above 12) are tracked with an owner and reported beside the outcomes.

DECISION RULES (set now): continue if at least 16 of 24 are observed using SBI at 90 days and item 7 does not fall. Revise if 10 to 15. Below 10, review workplace barriers before changing the course. No decision on fewer than 18 observed managers. Each finding is logged with the objective, the suspected design dimension, and an owner. Cohort 2 is compared with cohort 1 on the same measures and changes are logged.

DATA HANDLING: participants consent to observation and note sampling; results are reported in aggregate; individual records are kept 12 months and are not used in performance review.

expected_scores.rationale: Every link in the chain is either measured or set aside with a reason (results for O2, learning for O3). The objective-to-evidence table names a measure, a source, and an owner for each objective, with access confirmed. Timing covers baseline, end, and two delayed points; the role-play checklist was piloted with rater agreement stated; small numbers are reported as counts. Attribution is a 4, not a 5: the staggered cohort, the trend line, and the success cases are a sound quasi-experimental design with other explanations named, but the plan does not say how confident a claim it will allow itself. Workplace conditions are planned, owned, and reported beside outcomes. Thresholds for continue and revise, a minimum sample, routing, version comparison, and data handling are all stated in advance.

edge_cases.label: Good: Impact report scored against its own measurement plan, with honest limits
edge_cases.description: The 90-day impact report for the same programme. It reports against the thresholds the plan set, names what it could not show, and routes each finding back to the design.
edge_cases.input: Impact report for a new-manager programme, 14 weeks after cohort 2 ended. Stage: post_launch. The measurement plan agreed before launch is supplied as the reference.
edge_cases.artifact:
IMPACT REPORT - New Manager Programme, cohorts 1 and 2 (24 managers)

ANSWER FOR THE DECISION-MAKER: revise, do not retire. The plan's threshold for 'continue' was 16 of 24 managers observed using SBI at 90 days. We observed 21 managers; 13 used it. That is in the 'revise' band (10 to 15).

CHAIN
Participation: 24 of 24 completed. Reaction: reported in the appendix; not used as evidence.
Learning: role-play checklist, 22 of 24 met the standard at the end of the programme.
Behavior: senior-manager observation at 30 days (15 of 22 observed using SBI) and 90 days (13 of 21). Calendar data: weekly 1:1s held with every direct report rose from 7 of 24 managers at baseline to 19 at 30 days and 17 at 90 days. Delegation log samples: 14 of 20 sampled entries had an outcome, deadline, and check-in.
Results: engagement item 7 moved from 3.4 to 3.6 across the participating teams. The four prior cycles ranged from 3.3 to 3.5, so this is at the top of the usual range, not clearly outside it.

WHAT WE CAN AND CANNOT CLAIM
At 30 days, 8 of 11 observed cohort-1 managers used SBI; cohort 2, not yet trained, had 2 of 12. That gap is the strongest evidence that the programme changed behavior. We cannot claim an effect on engagement: the change is within the prior range and the pay review landed in the same quarter. Three managers were not observed at 90 days (two changed role, one on leave); if all three had stopped using SBI the count would still be 13 of 24.

WHY IT WORKED WHERE IT DID (success and non-success cases, 6 interviews)
The three strongest cases all had a senior manager who asked about the commitment in their own 1:1. The three weakest all had spans of control above 12 and said they had no time. Workplace conditions reported beside outcomes: 18 of 24 senior managers attended the briefing; of the 13 managers using SBI at 90 days, 12 had a briefed senior manager.

FINDINGS ROUTED TO THE DESIGN
1. Evidence: 9 of 22 role-plays lost marks on the 'impact' step. Objective: O1. Suspected cause: practice gave feedback on structure, not on naming impact. Change: add a worked example and a second practice. Owner: course owner, before cohort 3.
2. Evidence: SBI use fell from 15 to 13 between day 30 and day 90. Objective: O1. Suspected cause: prompts stop at week 9. Change: add prompts at weeks 12 and 16. Owner: L&D operations.
3. Evidence: all three weakest cases have spans above 12. Not a course problem. Routed to the HR business partner as an open barrier from the needs analysis.

DATA HANDLING: results are aggregate; no individual is named; observation records will be deleted 12 months after collection as the plan stated. Cohort 3 will be compared on the same measures.

expected_scores.rationale: The report follows the chain the plan set out and keeps reaction in proportion. Every objective is reported against the measure the plan named. Measurement is a 4: baseline, end, and two delayed points with observation and system evidence, and non-response is examined, but the engagement measure is a single survey item and observer agreement in the field is not reported. Attribution is a 4: the staggered cohort is a real comparison and the report declines the engagement claim, naming the pay review; it is not a 5 because the comparison covers one behavior at one time point. Workplace conditions are reported beside outcomes and explain the pattern. The result is read against the thresholds set in advance, each finding names an objective, a suspected cause, a change, and an owner, and the data handling matches the plan.

edge_cases.label: Borderline: Careful measures and comparison, but the workplace and the decision are missing
edge_cases.description: An analytically strong plan for a sales enablement course. It measures learning and behavior well and has a comparison, but treats transfer as the learner's job and never says what result would change anything.
edge_cases.input: Measurement plan for a product-launch sales enablement course, 180 account executives across six regions. Stage: pre_launch.
edge_cases.artifact:
MEASUREMENT PLAN - Product launch enablement

OBJECTIVES AND MEASURES: each of the five talking points is mapped to a call-review item (table attached). Product knowledge check at the end of the course, 20 scenario items written to the objectives. Call reviews by sales operations at two and six weeks after launch, 4 calls per executive, scored on the five items. Conversion on the new product from the CRM, weekly.

BASELINE AND COMPARISON: conversion on the previous comparable launch is the baseline. Regions 1 to 3 take the course in week one and regions 4 to 6 in week four, so weeks one to three give a comparison. Other factors noted: the regional pricing promotion in region 2 and the usual quarter-end rise.

SAMPLE: all 180 executives; 720 reviewed calls per wave. Reviewer agreement was checked on 30 calls.

CHAIN: completion and a three-question reaction survey are collected. Results measure is conversion on the new product.

AFTER THE COURSE: executives are expected to apply the talking points. A reminder email goes out in week two. Managers will be told the course has launched.

REPORTING: a dashboard for the sales leadership team, refreshed weekly, with region and individual views. Findings will be discussed at the quarterly business review.

expected_scores.rationale: The chain reaches results with a measure tied to the launch goal, and behavior is observed, not self-reported; no rationale is given for the links chosen, so 4. Each talking point maps to a call-review item with a named source, but owners and identifiers are not stated. Measurement has a baseline, an end check, and two delayed points with checked reviewer agreement; the knowledge check is not piloted. The staggered regions are a real comparison and two other explanations are named. Transfer is a 2: use is assumed, follow-up is one reminder email, and managers are only told the course exists. Decision is a 2: the decision is implied, nothing says what result triggers a change or who owns it, and the individual views on a leadership dashboard have no stated limits on use.

edge_cases.label: Borderline: Honest post-launch review that rests on before/after and self-report
edge_cases.description: A post-launch review of a compliance course. Learning is measured against objectives and there is a delayed measure, but behavior is self-reported and the only comparison is before and after.
edge_cases.input: Post-launch review of an annual data-handling compliance course, 2,400 staff, 12 weeks after launch. Stage: post_launch. No measurement plan was written before launch.
edge_cases.artifact:
POST-LAUNCH REVIEW - Data handling course

Completion: 2,310 of 2,400 (96%). Satisfaction: 4.1 of 5 (response rate 38%).
Learning: the end-of-course scenario check is written to the six policy objectives; mean 84%, and objective 4 (sharing data with suppliers) is the weakest at 61%.
Follow-up at 8 weeks: a survey asked staff whether they had changed how they handle data. 620 replied (26%); 71% said yes. The same survey repeated four scenario items; scores held at 80%.
Results: reported data-handling incidents were 41 in the quarter before launch and 29 in the quarter after. We note that the incident reporting form also changed during this period, which may affect the count.
Managers were sent a briefing note before launch. A job aid for supplier requests was added to the intranet.
Recommendation: keep the course. Rework the supplier-sharing section, since objective 4 scored lowest. The course owner will review the results.
Data: results are reported by department, not by individual.

expected_scores.rationale: A consistent 3. The chain has learning measured against objectives, behavior from self-report only, and a results measure that is named and loosely linked. Most objectives map to a measure, with item-level results for the weakest, but there is no objective-to-evidence table and the sources are not owned. There is one delayed measure, the response rate is reported, and the behavior measure is self-report of use. The comparison is before and after only; the change to the reporting form is mentioned and the claim stays modest. Managers were informed and one support was added, with nothing measured. The decision is stated after the data arrived and routed to the course owner, with one finding tied to a section of the course and aggregate reporting. Severity flag: behavior from self-report alone.

edge_cases.label: Bad: 'Measurement plan' that is the platform's default report
edge_cases.description: A plan for a year-long leadership programme that lists what the learning platform records by default and calls it measurement.
edge_cases.input: Measurement plan for a 12-month leadership programme, 300 participants, budget of several hundred thousand. Stage: pre_launch.
edge_cases.artifact:
MEASUREMENT PLAN - Leadership Excellence Programme

We will track success using LMS data. Metrics: enrolments, completions, time spent, logins per week, and the end-of-module quiz scores. A satisfaction survey will go out after each module. We expect high engagement.

Impact: the programme will improve leadership capability across the business and support retention. We will report progress to the executive team each quarter.

Participants are responsible for applying what they learn. Line managers have been told the programme is running.

expected_scores.rationale: For a programme of this size and cost the plan is far out of proportion. The chain stops at completion, satisfaction, and end-of-module quizzes, with results asserted. No objective is mapped to anything; the data is whatever the platform records by default, at course and module level. Everything is collected at the end of each module, with recall quizzes and satisfaction. There is no baseline, no comparison, and impact is asserted in advance. Managers are mentioned and use is assumed. Quarterly reporting is the end product: no decision rule, no routing, nothing on learner data. Severity flags: completion or satisfaction as effectiveness; nothing measured after the course ends; objectives with no evidence; no route back to the design.

edge_cases.label: Bad: Return-on-investment figure with no baseline, comparison, or account of other causes
edge_cases.description: An impact report that credits a revenue rise to a negotiation course and quotes a return figure, from after-only data and a self-estimate survey.
edge_cases.input: Impact report for a two-day negotiation skills course, 85 account managers, six months after delivery. Stage: post_launch. No measurement plan was supplied.
edge_cases.artifact:
IMPACT REPORT - Negotiation Skills

HEADLINE: 412% return on investment.

Revenue from the 85 trained account managers in the six months after the course was 6.2M. The course cost 310K. Participants were asked in a survey how much of their recent success they would put down to the course; the 31 who replied gave an average of 26%. Applying that share to revenue gives 1.6M of benefit, a return of 412%.

Participants rated the course 4.5 of 5. 90% said they were more confident negotiating. Several said they now use the techniques daily.

A new pricing structure and two large renewals also landed in this period.

Conclusion: the course has paid for itself four times over and should be rolled out to all 400 customer-facing staff.

expected_scores.rationale: The report has reaction and a results number but nothing between them: learning was not measured and behavior rests on a few remarks. No objective is mapped to any evidence. Measurement is confidence and satisfaction plus a self-estimate from 31 of 85 with no look at who did not reply. Attribution is a 1: a causal claim and a return figure from after-only revenue, with the pricing change and the large renewals named and then ignored. The workplace is not considered. A decision is implied (roll out to 400) but with no threshold and no route back to the design. Severity flags: attribution without comparison; behavior from self-report alone; completion or satisfaction as effectiveness.

edge_cases.label: Bad (built to tempt): Polished completion dashboard presented as proof of impact
edge_cases.description: A well-produced, data-rich dashboard summary. It is precise, segmented, and confident, and every number in it is about activity. Built to test whether a judge mistakes polish and volume of data for evidence. Expected overall at or below 3.0.
edge_cases.input: Executive dashboard summary for a cybersecurity awareness course, 5,200 staff, presented to the board as evidence of impact. Stage: post_launch. No measurement plan was supplied.
edge_cases.artifact:
SECURITY AWARENESS - IMPACT DASHBOARD (Q3)

PROVEN IMPACT AT A GLANCE
- Completion: 96.4% (5,013 of 5,200), up 11 points on last year. All 14 departments above 90%.
- Average quiz score: 91.2%. First-attempt pass rate: 88%.
- Learner satisfaction: 4.7 of 5 (n = 3,870, response rate 74%). Net promoter score +52.
- Average time in module: 23 min 40 s (target 25 min). Median completion: day 9 of a 30-day window.
- Engagement index (logins x interactions x completion): 87, top quartile against the vendor benchmark.

SEGMENT VIEWS: heat map of completion by department, site, grade, and tenure, with drill-down to named individuals and a ranked league table of the slowest completers for their managers.

TREND: completion has risen every quarter for six quarters. Phishing-related incidents logged by the service desk were lower this quarter than last, demonstrating that the course is working.

DATA QUALITY: all figures are drawn directly from the learning platform and refreshed nightly. Confidence interval on satisfaction: plus or minus 0.03.

CONCLUSION: with near-universal completion, strong scores, and falling incidents, the course has demonstrably reduced the organisation's security risk. Recommend renewing the three-year licence.

expected_scores.rationale: Every number here is accurate and none of it answers the question. The chain is completion, satisfaction, and an end-of-course quiz, with the result asserted (2). Nothing is mapped to an objective; the data is the platform's course-level totals, however finely segmented (1). All measures are taken at the end of the course; the high response rate and narrow interval describe the satisfaction survey, not learning or behavior (2). The fall in incidents is credited to the course from one quarter-on-quarter change with no baseline design and no other explanation considered (1). The workplace is not considered (1). The dashboard is the end product, with no decision rule set in advance, and it exposes named individuals in a league table for managers (1). A judge that scores this above 3.0 is rewarding presentation. Severity flags: completion or satisfaction as effectiveness; nothing measured after the course ends; objectives with no evidence; attribution without comparison; learner data misuse.

edge_cases.label: Bad (built to tempt): Warm, well-argued renewal case that rests on satisfaction alone
edge_cases.description: A persuasive renewal case for a wellbeing and resilience programme. The writing is sincere, the testimonials are moving, and the sponsor is supportive. The evidence is satisfaction and attendance. Built to test whether a judge is carried by tone and stakeholder approval. Expected overall at or below 3.0.
edge_cases.input: Renewal case for a resilience programme, 640 participants over one year, submitted to the budget committee. Stage: post_launch. No measurement plan was supplied.
edge_cases.artifact:
RENEWAL CASE - Resilience at Work

In its first year the programme reached 640 colleagues across every function, with 92% attending all four sessions. It is the highest-rated programme we have ever run: 4.8 of 5 overall, and 97% would recommend it to a colleague. The feedback has been overwhelming.

IN PARTICIPANTS' WORDS
'This is the first training that felt like it was for me.' 'I use the breathing technique every day.' 'My whole team is calmer.' 'Honestly life-changing.'

The Chief People Officer has called it 'a flagship for our culture', and line managers have been very supportive. Demand for next year already exceeds places.

Voluntary turnover fell from 14% to 12% this year, and we believe the programme played an important part.

We considered a follow-up survey but did not want to burden participants. Given the exceptional response, we ask the committee to renew for three years and double the number of places.

expected_scores.rationale: The chain is attendance and satisfaction; learning was not measured, behavior is four quotations, and the result is asserted (2, on the completion-plus-satisfaction anchor, with no quiz even). No objective is stated or mapped (1). The only instrument is an end-of-session satisfaction survey, and a later measure was considered and dropped (1). The fall in turnover is credited to the programme with no baseline design, no comparison, and no other explanation (1). Manager support is mentioned, not planned or measured (2). A decision is implied, with no threshold set in advance and no route to the design (2). High ratings, strong demand, and a senior sponsor are reasons people like the programme, not evidence that it changed anything. A judge that scores this above 3.0 is being carried by tone. Severity flags: completion or satisfaction as effectiveness; nothing measured after the course ends; attribution without comparison; behavior from self-report alone.
